title: Art and music debates
hook: scholars differ on musical instruments, while nasheed and recitation flourish

segments.voice: Yesterday, women scholars today, and the women of Medina who asked for a day of their own. Your line was she teaches. Whose name did you learn? Day one thousand four hundred.

It's Eid in Medina, and in 'Aisha's house two girls are singing. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is lying down nearby, his face turned away. Then Abu Bakr walks in, 'Aisha's father, and he's shocked. Musical instruments of Satan, he says, in the house of the Messenger of Allah? The Prophet turns toward him and says, in paraphrase: leave them, Abu Bakr. Every people has its feast day, and this is ours. The report is in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aisha herself. And it sits right in the middle of a question Muslims still discuss: what place does music have?
screen: `TWO GIRLS SINGING ON EID.` → `ABU BAKR OBJECTS.` → `LEAVE THEM. THIS IS OUR FEAST.`

segments.voice: Here is where scholars differ. Al-Bukhari also records a saying, in a chapter on drinks, that some of the Prophet's community will one day treat as lawful silk, wine and musical instruments. Some scholars read this as forbidding instruments, and they allow only the voice, and perhaps a simple frame drum at weddings and on Eid. Other scholars question how that report reaches al-Bukhari, or read it as condemning a whole scene of drinking and excess rather than the instruments alone, and they allow music whose words and setting are clean. Both sides are reading the same collection carefully. Neither is careless about the faith. Now turn to the voice. Nasheed, songs sung with the voice alone, or with a drum, are sung at weddings, in school halls and in headphones. And there is recitation of the Qur'an. In Pickthall's translation, the Prophet is told to "chant the Qur'an in measured cadence." Al-Bukhari keeps a report in which the Prophet hears Abu Musa reciting and tells him, in paraphrase, that he has been given a flute from among the flutes of the family of David. The praise for a beautiful voice compares it to a musical instrument. So the debate about instruments goes on, held in good faith, and the voices keep rising. This week began with one moon and many views and ends with music. It also closes this stretch of questions of today: science reading signs, health as a trust, stewards not owners, the tongue with thumbs, and now voices.
screen: `SILK, WINE AND INSTRUMENTS.` · `TWO READINGS, BOTH IN GOOD FAITH.` · `NASHEED: THE VOICE ALONE.` · `A FLUTE OF THE FAMILY OF DAVID.` · then, large: `CHANT THE QUR'AN IN MEASURED CADENCE.`

segments.voice: The practice: respect a view on music. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone whose view on music differs from yours, stricter or looser. A parent, a friend, a teacher, someone at the mosque, or simply a stranger whose choice you've noticed. Picture them choosing as they do because they're trying to be careful with something they love. Hold that for a few breaths without arguing. If you like, let a voice you love play quietly in your memory, a recitation, a lullaby, a nasheed, a song from home. If you pray, you can give thanks for voices. The bell holds the time.
Art and music debates. Scholars differ over musical instruments, in good faith, while nasheed and the recited Qur'an keep voices rising. Today's word.

Your line: views differ, voices rise. Today, listen to one recitation or one nasheed all the way through, and leave someone else's view on music alone. Tomorrow, bringing it home. Day one thousand four hundred.

howItsDone: Muslims hold different views on musical instruments: some avoid them and listen only to the voice or a frame drum, others enjoy music they consider clean in words and setting, and recitation of the Qur'an and nasheed are part of daily life for people holding either view.

notes: Confirm Bukhari 952, 5590 and 5048, and Pickthall's wording of 73:4.

Bukhari 5590 is a mu'allaq report (without a fully connected chain at that point in al-Bukhari); the script says only that some scholars 'question how that report reaches al-Bukhari'. Confirm that both positions are fairly represented and not ranked.
'Allow only the voice, and perhaps a simple frame drum at weddings and on Eid' summarizes the stricter view; confirm.
